title: My Opinion on Technology in Education
writingModel: Technology in Education: A Tool, Not a Teacher — by Kamila Seitkali

In my opinion, technology is one of the most powerful tools available to students today — but only when it is used wisely. The debate about technology in education is often framed as a simple choice between "more technology" and "less technology." I think this framing misses the point entirely.

The benefits of technology in education are real and significant. Students now have access to resources that previous generations could not have imagined. A student in Uralsk can watch a lecture by a professor in London. Khan Academy, Coursera, and dozens of other platforms offer world-class content for free. For students in countries like Kazakhstan, where access to specialised expertise may be limited, the internet has been genuinely transformative.

However, technology in education is not without its problems. Research shows that students who handwrite their notes retain more than those who type. Multitasking — switching between lecture content and a social media feed — reduces comprehension, even when students believe they are managing both well. The presence of a smartphone on a desk reduces cognitive performance, even if the phone is not being used. These are not small effects.

I strongly believe that the key is conscious, intentional use. A student who uses a laptop to take structured notes, access primary sources, and collaborate on shared documents is using technology well. A student who uses the same laptop to browse social media during a lecture is wasting an expensive tool and, more importantly, their own time.

On the other hand, I recognise that banning technology from lectures is not necessarily the answer either. The digital world is the world that students will work in. Learning to manage digital distractions, to choose focus over convenience, to use AI as a tool rather than a replacement for thinking — these are skills that students need to develop, not avoid.

To sum up, I believe that technology in education is neither a blessing nor a curse. It is what we make of it. The most important skill is not knowing how to use the tools — it is knowing when to use them, when to put them down, and why.
